1973.websynth.zip.blurb: A project bundle, so its sampled parts travel inside the file.

1979.websynth.json.blurb: E dorian, with one note from outside it: the B flat in the bass walk-down, the blue flat five. The KEY tab lets it through as an extra note, so the key filter is on and the walk-down still plays as written. Set the extra note to none and the B flat snaps down to A.

1985-1.websynth.json.blurb: Half of a pair, Crockett's Theme: load 1985-2 on a second device, pair them over WiFi sync or MIDI and press Play on either one. This half is the groove: the octave bass pulse, the lead, the bridge guitar stabs and the drum kit. One patch plays both bass and lead, and velocity decides which one you hear: the filter envelope is negative, so a hard-hit note starts open and snaps shut, which is the bass pluck, while the soft lead barely closes and stays bright. With sustain at 1, a tied note is already where its envelopes are heading, so it holds without re-plucking. A motion lane mutes the lead through the opening progression. It plays complete on its own too.

1985-2.websynth.json.blurb: Half of a pair, Crockett's Theme: load 1985-1 on a second device, pair them over WiFi sync or MIDI and press Play on either one. This half is the strings and the same lead, over a percussion kit of cowbell, shakers, congas, bongo and clave. The sequencer runs at 1/8 over 16 cells, two bars a bank. The strings are a root and two inner voices, struck on the beat and held with ties. The swell into each verse is one held chord whose velocity climbs step by step. In the last verse the fourth track drops its string and doubles the lead an octave up. It plays complete on its own too.

Ageispolis-1.websynth.json.name: Ageispolis-1
Ageispolis-1.websynth.json.blurb: Half of a pair: load Ageispolis-2 on a second device, pair them over WiFi sync or MIDI and press Play on either one. This half is the melody and the chords: the tune on the first track, and an F minor that moves to B flat held under it on the other three, tied from step to step. It plays on its own too, without bass or drums.

Ageispolis-2.websynth.json.name: Ageispolis-2
Ageispolis-2.websynth.json.blurb: Half of a pair: load Ageispolis-1 on a second device, pair them over WiFi sync or MIDI and press Play on either one. This half is the bass, the strings and an 808 kit. The bass is the first track; the strings are three-note chords on the other three, held through every other bar. The closed hat chokes the open one. It plays on its own too, without the melody.

Ageispolis.websynth.zip.name: Ageispolis
Ageispolis.websynth.zip.blurb: The Ageispolis sync pair made into one file, so it needs only one device. Ageispolis-1 was rendered and recorded into a sampler slot of Ageispolis-2, so the melody and chords play as a sample alongside the bass, strings and 808 kit. Motion lanes then shape the arrangement and the mix across its 64 bars.

Around_the_World.websynth.json.name: Around the World
Around_the_World.websynth.json.blurb: The four sequencer tracks are the four instruments of the video — bass, the vocal, the guitar riff and the synth — playing one four-bar phrase, and motion lanes on the track mutes bring each part in and out, so the whole arrangement lives in the Motion card. Swing is at 27% for the lazy late 16ths of the pickups.

Blue_Monday.websynth.json.name: Blue Monday
Blue_Monday.websynth.json.blurb: Two four-bar halves: the pulsing sequence with its two out-of-phase lines, and the octave bass under the hook and the melody. The drums carry the breaks — the kick roll, the dotted stop, a 32nd-note kick ratchet and the snare-and-clap rolls — over bars where the sequencer rests.

Eleanor_Rigby-1.websynth.json.name: Eleanor Rigby-1
Eleanor_Rigby-1.websynth.json.blurb: Half of a pair: load Eleanor Rigby-2 on a second device, pair them over WiFi sync or MIDI and press Play on either one. This half is the low strings and the voice: the tune, the cello, the viola's lines and the second voice in the "Ah" sections. Its last verse has its own cello arpeggios, the cello doubling the tune and the A minor near the end. It plays complete on its own too.

Eleanor_Rigby-2.websynth.json.name: Eleanor Rigby-2
Eleanor_Rigby-2.websynth.json.blurb: Half of a pair: load Eleanor Rigby-1 on a second device, pair them over WiFi sync or MIDI and press Play on either one. This half is the violins: the same tune, the staccato chord stabs and a pizzicato root under each stab, so it has a bass line when it plays alone. In the last chorus it switches to the "Ah, look at all the lonely people" line while the other device carries the chorus, as on the record.

First_Light.websynth.json.name: First Light
First_Light.websynth.json.blurb: One riff, four chords: the whole progression is bar transposes on two banks. POLY filter, hat choke, tempo-locked LFO — and the arp is armed, so hold a key.

Gankogui.websynth.json.name: Gankogui
Gankogui.websynth.json.blurb: Twelve-eight, and three lanes on three different cycles: the bell locked to the 24-tick bar, the riff looping every 16 ticks and the motion lane every 18. The whole machine only lands together once every six bars.

Illusion_1.websynth.json.name: Illusion 1
Illusion_1.websynth.json.blurb: The Shepard scale: a scale that climbs forever and never gets anywhere. Every tone is six sine waves an octave apart, and a fixed filter shapes them into a bell, loudest in the middle and fading to nothing at both ends. As the scale rises, the top partials fade out while new ones fade in at the bottom, so after twelve steps the tone is exactly where it started, yet all you heard was it going up. Halfway through it turns round and falls forever instead.

Illusion_2.websynth.zip.name: Illusion 2
Illusion_2.websynth.zip.blurb: The Shepard–Risset glissando: the Shepard scale made continuous, an audio barber's pole. Eight sine waves an octave apart all slide upward together, and each one's loudness follows a fixed bell over pitch: it fades in at the bottom, swells through the middle and fades out at the top, where it slips back to the bottom unheard. So the sound keeps rising and never arrives. A synth voice cannot do this, because every partial would have to wrap at once, so this one is a project bundle: one sampler slot plays a sixteen-second loop that is exactly one octave of the climb, computed rather than recorded.

Illusion_3.websynth.zip.name: Illusion 3
Illusion_3.websynth.zip.blurb: Risset's accelerating rhythm: a breakbeat that speeds up forever. The same break plays at three tempos at once, each twice as fast as the last, and all three accelerate together, doubling every eight bars. Loudness follows a bell over tempo, like the Shepard tone's over pitch: the fastest copy fades out as it gets frantic, and a new slow one fades in underneath. After eight bars every copy has become the next one up, so the loop starts again without a seam. The hits are this synth's own drum machine, rendered once and laid out offline; one sampler slot plays the loop, because eight drum tracks cannot hold three copies of a kit.

Illusion_4.websynth.json.name: Illusion 4
Illusion_4.websynth.json.blurb: The tritone paradox, discovered by Diana Deutsch: each bar plays two Shepard tones a tritone apart, exactly half an octave. Built like Illusion 1, each tone has a note name but no octave, so neither tone is higher and the interval has no direction. Yet most people clearly hear some pairs go up and others go down, and two listeners often disagree about the same pair; which pairs rise seems to depend on the speech you grew up hearing. Listen with a friend, write down up or down for each of the twelve pairs, and compare.

Illusion_5.websynth.json.name: Illusion 5
Illusion_5.websynth.json.blurb: The missing fundamental: the same tune four times, and the pitch you hear never changes. First as pure sine waves, then with three harmonics added above each note. The third time, the note itself is gone and only harmonics 2, 3, 4 and 6 play; the fourth time, only 3, 4, 6 and 8. Your ear works out which note those harmonics belong to and hears it, though nothing is playing at that pitch. It is how a phone call keeps a man's voice deep, and laptop speakers can barely play the lowest notes here anyway.

Illusion_6.websynth.json.name: Illusion 6
Illusion_6.websynth.json.blurb: Auditory streaming: one note, a second note, the first again, a pause. While the two notes are close in pitch it is a single galloping rhythm. Every two bars the second note moves further away, and somewhere along the way the gallop falls apart into two separate lines: a fast, even pulse of the low note and a slow one of the high note. Then the interval shrinks again, and the two lines hold on longer than it took them to split before the gallop comes back.

Illusion_7.websynth.zip.name: Illusion 7
Illusion_7.websynth.zip.blurb: The continuity illusion: a tone gliding up and down, chopped into pieces. First the gaps are silent and the glide sounds broken. Then each gap is filled with a burst of noise, and the glide seems to carry on unbroken behind it, even though the tone stops completely while the noise plays; your brain fills in what the noise would have hidden. Last, the bursts are made too quiet to have hidden anything, and the gaps are back. A computed clip on one sampler slot, because the noise has to fit each gap exactly.

Illusion_8.websynth.zip.name: Illusion 8
Illusion_8.websynth.zip.blurb: The Zwicker tone: listen to the silence. Three six-second bursts of noise play, each with a band cut out of it: 2 to 4 kHz, 1 to 2 kHz, then everything above 3 kHz. After each burst comes six seconds of silence, and most people hear a faint, pure tone in it for a few seconds, pitched inside the missing band, though nothing is playing. Best in a quiet room at a moderate level. The bursts are computed clips on three sampler slots, since a band has to be removed completely for it to work.

Luftballons.websynth.json.name: Luftballons
Luftballons.websynth.json.blurb: 99 Luftballons, the verse is bass and drums with the guitar coming in. From the chorus on, all four POLY tracks play: the bass, the brass an octave above it and the two notes of the guitar's power chord, which ends on an A major triad over the bass in the fill. The sequencer runs at 1/8 over 16 cells, two bars a bank, and the snare's flam on the backbeat is a two-hit ratchet.

Maison.websynth.json.name: Maison
Maison.websynth.json.blurb: French house, built around the ducker: the kick keys it, everything else breathes. Two bars of silence, a filter riser, then the drop. Mute the drum lane and the pumping stops with it.

Nocturne.websynth.json.name: Nocturne
Nocturne.websynth.json.blurb: The long, slow one: four sequencer tracks through the POLY filter, with motion driving it.

Radio_Ga_Ga.websynth.zip.name: Radio Ga Ga
Radio_Ga_Ga.websynth.zip.blurb: A project bundle built from the song's outro. The first twelve bars are only the drum machine and the sixteenth-note synth pulse; then the band comes in. Piano, bass, Rhodes, strings, guitar and the cymbals were each played through this synth with their own patch, at the file's own timing, and recorded into a sampler slot — so the six parts sound together with the live synth and drums. The whole progression in the second half is one sequencer bank, transposed bar by bar. The sampled parts were recorded at 114 BPM, so at any other tempo they drift away from the synth and drums.

Run_Away_2.websynth.zip.name: Run Away 2
Run_Away_2.websynth.zip.blurb: The Run Away idea rebuilt as a project bundle, sampled parts alongside the synth.

Running_Up_That_Hill.websynth.json.name: Running Up That Hill
Running_Up_That_Hill.websynth.json.blurb: The drums are the song: a deep tom pattern in sixteenths, a kick on one and three and the crack on two and four, with a shaker and a clave standing in for the cabasa and woodblock. Over it, four tracks at 1/8 — bass, the hook, the strings' counter-line and the chord's top voice — each struck once and carried by a long release rather than held.

Slouch.websynth.json.name: Slouch
Slouch.websynth.json.blurb: Swing sits at zero — every bit of the drag is per-step micro-timing. The snare is five notches late, the clap trails it by another two, the kick pushes ahead, and one hi-hat lands a third of a step off.

Sweet_Dreams.websynth.json.name: Sweet Dreams
Sweet_Dreams.websynth.json.blurb: The sequencer runs at 1/8 over all 16 cells, so every bank holds two bars — the riff and the vocal line each fit one bank, which is how eight banks cover the whole song. Four POLY tracks: bass, both riff lines and the melody or chord on top.

Take_Me_On.websynth.zip.name: Take Me On
Take_Me_On.websynth.zip.blurb: Take on Me with a drum-and-bass break laid over its drums: a 170 BPM four-bar break, cut into its four bars and stretched to 175 without changing its pitch. Each bar has its own sampler slot, and sampler banks A to D each play one of them, so the chain A B C D plays the break back in order and reordering the chain rearranges it.

Take_on_Me.websynth.json.name: Take on Me
Take_on_Me.websynth.json.blurb: All sixteen banks, two bars each: the sequencer runs at 1/8 over 16 cells, so the intro, riff, verse, chorus and outro each fit as the arrangement's own bars rather than look-alikes. Each part keeps its own track — bass, the riff (brass in the chorus), the guitar's eighths and the strings or aahs on top — and the pad pulses in eighths because a held note would retrigger.

Tosti.websynth.json.name: Tosti
Tosti.websynth.json.blurb: Three sequencer tracks over a conga-and-clave kit.
